exposure: rooming-in status (with mothers vs. NICU admission)
mode of birth (normal delivery vs. cesarean section)
cohort: 180 newborn infants divided into three groups: normal delivery rooming-in with mothers, cesarean section rooming-in with mothers, and neonates admitted to NICU.
finding: Umbilical cord bacterial colonization, predominantly by Staphylococcus aureus, was more common in newborn infants born by cesarean section and rooming in with mothers compared to the other study groups.
mod_finding: Umbilical cord bacterial colonization was significantly more common in newborn infants born by cesarean section and rooming in with mothers compared to those born by normal delivery or admitted to the NICU.
cross-section timing: Bacterial cultures were performed on the second day for all groups, with an additional culture on days 5-7 for infants admitted to NICU.
gest_age: Normal gestational age (38 to 42 weeks) was observed in 67.2% of subjects, with significant differences in gestational age among the study groups.
